subtype: Approach: start with a tiny version that can be done on bad days [Action]
passage:
I'm Nikita, and I used to believe that if a workout wasn't an hour, it didn't count. So I did nothing for months. Then Vishal, my flatmate, said, "Just do ten minutes. Even when you feel awful."

So the first week I stretched for ten minutes, then jogged slowly to the end of the lane and back. It was almost embarrassing. But on the bad days, when I had a headache or a long day, I could still do that. The next week I added two minutes. The week after, two more.

Now it's forty minutes, three mornings a week, and I've not missed since the start. I didn't get fit by being brave. I got here by being small enough that I couldn't say no.

qa.q: How long was the first workout?
qa.a: Stretching for ten minutes, then a slow jog to the end of the lane and back.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel about the tiny first workout?
qa.a: Nikita found it almost embarrassing, though the small size meant it could be done even on bad days.

qa.q: What could Nikita do on a day when even ten minutes seems too much, and why?
qa.a: Nikita could do just the stretching or step outside for a minute, because keeping the chain unbroken matters more than the size of the session.

qa.q: How might Vishal see Nikita's progress?
qa.a: Vishal probably feels quietly pleased, having given the simple advice, and sees Nikita's steady mornings as proof that small steps last.

grounding: The person begins with ten minutes of stretching and a short jog instead of an hour at the gym, adding time each week.

passage:
I'm Sarika, and Elizabeth and I share a room at the working women's hostel in Chennai. In January she bought gym clothes and a membership and went twice. Then she stopped, embarrassed.
In February she tried something different. I watched it from my bed. She rolled a mat out between our cots and did ten minutes of stretching every morning, even on days she'd worked late. On Saturdays she added a short jog around the hostel compound, about six rounds.
Each Sunday she wrote something in a small notebook and added a little: two more minutes, one more round. By April the jog was twenty minutes and the stretches were a proper routine.
She never announced anything. But on the days she felt awful, she still did the ten minutes. I don't know what went on in her head, but she kept going.

qa.q: How many rounds did Elizabeth's first Saturday jogs cover?
qa.a: About six rounds of the hostel compound.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth likely feel after stopping the gym in January?
qa.a: She likely felt embarrassed and discouraged after going only twice.

qa.q: What else could Elizabeth add once the routine is steady?
qa.a: She could try one longer session a week, now that the daily habit is steady, so intensity comes after consistency.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth's new routine look to Sarika?
qa.a: Sarika sees a quiet, steady routine that survives even bad days, though Sarika can't know what Elizabeth is thinking.

grounding: Shows the person starting with ten minutes of stretching and a short jog instead of long gym sessions and adding time each week.

passage:
First week of June. Kavitha wanted to be fit but kept picturing hour-long gym sessions and giving up before starting. Her colleague Kishore said, "What's the smallest thing you'd do even on your worst day?" She said, "A few stretches for ten minutes, then a jog to the end of the lane and back." So that was the plan, every morning.
Third week. She had a fever for two days and still managed the stretching in bed on one of them. The jog was a slow walk. She ticked it off anyway. Each Sunday she added two minutes to the jog.
End of July. The jog now went round the whole block, twenty minutes. She'd missed only three days in eight weeks. Kishore asked if she'd join the office gym now. "Maybe later," she said. "This is what's working."

qa.q: How many days did Kavitha miss in eight weeks?
qa.a: She missed only three days in eight weeks.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha keep giving up before starting, and what was she feeling?
qa.a: She felt daunted and discouraged, picturing hour-long gym sessions that seemed too big to begin.

qa.q: What else could Kavitha try once the twenty-minute jog feels easy?
qa.a: She could add one short strength session a week, building on the steady habit instead of jumping to long gym hours.

qa.q: How might Kishore see Kavitha's progress?
qa.a: Kishore, who suggested the smallest version, would likely feel pleased that his question led to a habit that lasted.

grounding: Shows the person starting with a tiny ten-minute stretch and short jog that fits bad days and adding a little time each week.
